facts.text: Sir John Harington, an English courtier, described an early flush toilet in a book published in the 1590s.
Harington installed one of his flushing devices for Queen Elizabeth I, who was his godmother.
Harington's design included a valve and a system that washed waste down with water.
In 1775 Alexander Cumming, a Scottish watchmaker, received the first UK patent for a flushing water closet.
Cumming's invention centred on an S-shaped trap, or U-bend, in the pipe; his patent called it a stink trap, a water seal that keeps drain smells out.
In 1778 Joseph Bramah patented an improved flushing closet worked by a handle; by 1797 he had made and sold more than 6,000 closets.
When Cumming received his patent, houses had no indoor plumbing and there were no sewers for flushed waste to flow into.
In London, waste was traditionally collected in cesspools under or near houses and removed by night soil men.
Each flush of a water closet sent two gallons or more of water into the cesspool, filling it quickly with liquid that leaked into the soil.
Leaking cesspools contaminated underground springs and wells used for drinking water, carrying diseases such as cholera and typhoid into homes.
London's public sewers had originally been meant to carry away rainwater.
In 1815 London authorities first allowed cesspools and house drains to be connected to the public sewers; in 1847 such connection became required by law.
The public sewers emptied into the Thames, so between 1815 and 1847 the river changed from fairly clean to an open sewer.
Water discharged into the rivers also polluted the rivers from which London drew its water supply.
Almost 40,000 people died in London in four cholera epidemics during the 19th century.
Most people of the time, including members of Parliament, believed diseases spread through foul-smelling air rather than polluted water; this belief was later shown to be wrong.
The hot, dry summer of 1858 brought the Great Stink; members of Parliament were unable to stay in committee rooms and the library because of the smell from the river.
Parliament then passed a bill that allowed engineer Joseph Bazalgette to start building his sewer system at once; work began in January 1859.
Bazalgette's intercepting sewers ran parallel to the Thames and carried sewage east to outfalls at Beckton and Crossness, away from central London.
London's last cholera epidemic, in the summer of 1866, struck about one square mile of Whitechapel in the east, the only part of the system not yet complete.
World Toilet Day is observed every year on 19 November.
According to WHO/UNICEF figures cited by the UN, about 3.4 billion people, or 4 in 10 worldwide, lack safe toilets.
The World Bank indicator counts people using at least basic sanitation: improved sanitation facilities that are not shared with other households.
Derived from the dataset: in 2024 South Asia (82.0%) was just below the world share (82.2%); Sub-Saharan Africa (37.1%) left about 62.9% of people without at least basic sanitation.
